newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU start best without Italy-Belgian NBB quoted.
newsitem.headline: EMU start best without Italy-Belgian NBB quoted.

text.p: Europe's planned monetary union would best start without Italy since the country will not be able to meet the entry criterion on budget deficits, the Belgian central bank governor was quoted on Tuesday as saying.

Belgian newspaper De Financieel Economische Tijd quoted Alfons Verplaetse as saying, "I would not mind seeing countries with a government deficit of seven percent (of gross domestic product) lowering their deficit to three percent in a year's time and in a durable way. In my view that is not possible."
The paper concluded Verplaetse was speaking about Italy.
The central bank could not immediately confirm the report.
Verplaetse had been speaking in Antwerp where he presented the central bank's 1996 annual report, released in Brussels last week.
Italy's 1996 budget deficit has been estimated at close to seven percent of GDP. It aims to cut the ratio to three percent in 1997 to be able to join EMU from the planned start in 1999.

The Maastricht Treaty sets three percent as the ceiling for the deficit/GDP ratio as a requirement for entry to the single currency. Other criteria concern debt levels, and currency, interest rate and inflation stability.
Verplaetse was sceptical about an Italian plan to set a one-time euro tax to raise revenue to cut the 1997 deficit.
"To raise taxes and promise that you partly pay them back next year...personally I feel a bit uneasy about that," the paper quoted him as saying.
Analysts have criticised the plan for being at odds with the Maastricht Treaty's emphasis on durable economic convergence.
An EU ruling on this and various other budgetary practices governments have used to bring deficits down to three percent of GDP is due later this week.
Financial markets are sceptical Italy and other Mediterranean countries have the track record to ensure a stable single currency, as desired by Germany in particular.

Political leaders will choose the first group of nations to adopt the new currency early next year. It is largely expected to include a core of Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg as well as a few others.
